title: Gurung culture and the Gurkha story
meta_description: Who the Gurung (Tamu) people are, their priests, songs and villages below the Annapurnas, and how two centuries of Gurkha service shaped Ghandruk and Pokhara.
summary: The Gurung, who call themselves Tamu, are the people of the hills below Annapurna and Lamjung Himal, with their own language, priests and festivals. For two centuries their young men have served as Gurkhas in the British and Indian armies, and that service built many of the villages, schools and lodges trekkers see today.

sections.heading: Who the Tamu are
paras: Walk up from Pokhara toward Ghandruk, Landruk, Dhampus or Sikles and most of the families you meet are Gurung. They call themselves Tamu and their language Tamu kyi, a Tibeto-Burman language related to Thakali and Tamang, quite different from Nepali. The Gurung homeland is the middle hills of central Nepal: Kaski and Lamjung above all, with large communities in Gorkha, Syangja, Tanahun and Parbat. The Nyeshangba of upper Manang are sometimes grouped with them but have their own language and history.

Traditionally the Gurung were farmers and herders who moved flocks of sheep between high summer pastures and lower winter grazing, and grew millet, maize, barley and buckwheat on terraces cut into steep slopes. Many still do, but today village incomes come as much from tourism, overseas work and military pensions as from fields. Villages such as Ghandruk are known for being tidy and well organised, with stone-paved paths, community water taps and mothers' groups that run festivals and keep the trails clean.

sections.heading: Priests, gods and the cycle of life
paras: Gurung religion is layered. Most families follow Tibetan Buddhism, and lamas lead many rituals, but older than both Buddhism and Hinduism in the hills are the Gurung's own priests: the pachyu and the klehpree, sometimes written ghyabri. They chant long oral texts, in an old form of the language, that tell of the origins of the Tamu, guide the souls of the dead and protect households from harm. Some families also call Brahmin priests for Hindu ceremonies, and many celebrate Dashain and Tihar with their neighbours.

The most important Gurung rite is the pae or arghun, the final funeral ceremony held some time after a death to send the soul to the land of the ancestors. It can last several days and draws relatives from across the hills and abroad. A dummy figure of the dead person, dressed in their clothes, is the centre of the rite, and dancers, drummers and priests accompany it. If you are invited to one, it is a great honour; ask your guide how to behave.

The Gurung New Year, Tamu Lhosar, falls on the fifteenth day of the Nepali month of Poush, around 30 December. In Pokhara and the villages it brings processions in traditional dress, dances and family feasts. It is a national holiday in Nepal.

sections.heading: Songs, cloth and the village day
paras: Evenings in a Gurung village used to belong to the rodhi, a gathering of young men and women who met in a house to sing, work and court, sometimes through the night, swapping teasing verses in a sung conversation called dohori. Rodhi houses are rarer now, but the songs survive in cultural programmes, and some villages host an evening for visitors. The ghatu dance, performed by young girls in a trance-like state to tell an old story of a queen, is a Gurung tradition of Lamjung and Kaski in spring.

Gurung women are fine weavers. The bhangra, a sleeveless cloth tied over the shoulder and used to carry loads or worn as a wrap, is woven from allo, the fibre of the giant Himalayan nettle, on a back-strap loom. Men wear the bhoto, a short cross-tied jacket, and the kachhad, a wrap, with a khukuri at the waist on festival days. Women wear a velvet blouse, gold or coral jewellery, and a large gold ear ornament.

Food is simple and good: dhido made from millet or buckwheat, gundruk, a soup of fermented dried greens, kodo ko roti, millet flatbread, and the home-made millet liquor that hosts may offer to welcome guests. Refusing politely is fine.

sections.heading: The Gurkha story
paras: In 1814 the British East India Company went to war with the Kingdom of Nepal. The fighting in the hills, at forts such as Nalapani, impressed British officers so much that even before the war ended in 1816 they had begun recruiting Nepali hill soldiers into their own army. The name Gurkha comes from Gorkha, the hill kingdom of the Shah kings, and the first recruits were drawn largely from Gurung, Magar, Rai and Limbu communities.

For the next two centuries Gurkha regiments served in almost every British campaign, from the Indian rebellion of 1857 to both world wars, the Falklands and Afghanistan. Gurkha soldiers have been awarded the Victoria Cross, Britain's highest award for gallantry, many times. When India became independent in 1947 an agreement between Britain, India and Nepal divided the Gurkha regiments: some went to the British Army and the larger share to the new Indian Army, where Gurkhas still serve in large numbers. Singapore's police also recruits Gurkhas.

In 2009, after a long public campaign, the British government agreed that Gurkhas who retired before 1997 could settle in the United Kingdom. Many families now live between a village in Kaski and a town in England, and that link shows in the houses, schools and lodges of Ghandruk and Pokhara.

sections.heading: Recruitment in Pokhara
paras: The British Army still selects Gurkha recruits in Nepal, and the final selection takes place at the British Gurkhas camp in Pokhara. Thousands of young men apply each year for a few hundred places. One of the best-known tests is the doko race, an uphill run carrying a traditional basket loaded with about 25 kg. In the months before selection you may see young men training on the hills around Pokhara at dawn, running steps with weighted baskets.

For a hill family, a son in the British or Indian Army meant a regular wage, a pension and status in the village. Pension money built water systems, schools and the first lodges on the trekking routes. When you sleep in a lodge in Ghandruk or Chhomrong, there is a fair chance that it was started with a soldier's savings.

The word for such a man in Nepali is lahure, from Lahore, where hill men once served in the army of the Sikh ruler Ranjit Singh. Songs about the lahure who goes far away and the family waiting at home are still sung at village gatherings, and a soldier coming home on leave is still a big event in a hill village.

sections.heading: Words you will hear
paras: A few Gurung and Nepali words make conversations easier and more fun. Your hosts will be delighted if you try them.

sections.heading: Where to meet Gurung culture
paras: The easiest places to see Gurung life on a trip from Pokhara are on the trekking routes and in the city itself.

The best way, though, is simply to slow down. Spend two nights in one village rather than one night in each, sit in the kitchen while dinner is cooked, and ask your hosts about their grandparents. Many older Gurung men and women have remarkable stories of the war years, of herding sheep in the high pastures and of carrying loads to Pokhara before there were roads.
list: Ghandruk: the largest Gurung village in Kaski, with a museum of household objects and homestays in the old village.
Landruk and Dhampus: smaller ridge villages on the way to Australian Camp and the Modi Khola.
Sikles: a large Gurung village north-east of Pokhara below Lamjung Himal, less visited.
Gurkha Memorial Museum, Pokhara: medals, uniforms and stories of Gurkha service.
Tamu Lhosar in Pokhara at the end of December, with processions and dances.
Ask before photographing people, especially at rituals; remove shoes in kitchens and never step over the hearth.

faqs.q: Who are the Gurung people of Nepal?
faqs.a: The Gurung, who call themselves Tamu, are an ethnic group of the central hills of Nepal, especially Kaski and Lamjung districts below the Annapurnas. They speak a Tibeto-Burman language, follow a mix of Buddhism, their own priestly traditions and Hindu festivals, and are known for farming, herding, weaving and service in Gurkha regiments.

No. Gurkha soldiers have come from several hill communities, especially Gurung, Magar, Rai and Limbu, and today recruits come from many backgrounds across Nepal. The name Gurkha comes from Gorkha, the hill kingdom of the Shah dynasty, not from the Gurung people. Gurungs have, however, made up a large share of recruits for two centuries.

faqs.q: Where is the Gurkha Museum in Pokhara?
faqs.a: The Gurkha Memorial Museum is in Pokhara city, a short taxi ride from Lakeside. It displays medals, uniforms, photographs and stories from two centuries of Gurkha service, including Victoria Cross holders. Allow an hour or two. It pairs well with a visit to the old bazaar and the Bindhyabasini temple.

Tamu Lhosar, the Gurung New Year, is celebrated on the fifteenth day of the Nepali month of Poush, which usually falls around 30 December. In Pokhara there are processions, cultural programmes and dances, and families hold feasts. It is a public holiday in Nepal. Dates follow the Nepali calendar, so check before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I stay with a Gurung family?
faqs.a: Yes. Homestays in Ghandruk, Landruk, Dhampus and other Gurung villages welcome guests, and some are run by village committees. You sleep in a family home, eat with the family and join daily life. Rooms are simple, with shared bathrooms. A guide helps with language and customs and is required inside the conservation area.

A pachyu is one of the traditional priests of the Gurung people, along with the klehpree. They chant long oral texts in an old form of the Gurung language, conduct funeral rites and household rituals, and preserve stories of Tamu origins. Their tradition is older than Buddhism among the Gurung and is still practised in villages today.

faqs.q: What is the doko race in Gurkha selection?
faqs.a: It is a well-known part of British Army Gurkha selection in Pokhara: an uphill run carrying a traditional doko basket loaded with about 25 kg. It tests the strength and endurance that hill life builds. Young men train for months on the slopes around Pokhara before selection. Details of the tests can change from year to year.

Gurkhas earned respect through two centuries of service in British and Indian regiments, in both world wars and many later conflicts, with many awards for bravery including the Victoria Cross. Their motto, better to die than be a coward, is widely known. In Nepal, service also brought income that shaped hill villages.

faqs.q: What should I know before visiting a Gurung village?
faqs.a: Ask before photographing people, dress modestly, remove shoes before entering kitchens, and never step over or throw rubbish into the hearth, which is respected as pure. Accept tea or food with the right hand. If offered home-made liquor, a polite refusal is fine. Small gifts are welcome but not expected.
